pages.text:
Z-Transform for Discrete-Time Signals

Z-Transform is applicable for discrete-time intervals.

Time → Frequency

Continuous-time case:
CTFT is a generalization of LT.

Mapping:
( j\omega \longleftrightarrow s = \sigma + j\omega )

Laplace Transform gives more complete information about signals.

Discrete-time case:
DTFT is a generalization of Z-Transform.

DTFT definition:
( X(\omega) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j\omega n} )

x[n] may not be summable → DTFT may not exist.

Mapping:
( e^{j\omega} \rightarrow z )

( e^{j\omega} = z )

If ( |z| = 1 ), we get DTFT.
If ( |z| \neq 1 ), we get Z-Transform.

In LT, we worked with rectangular coordinates:
( s = \sigma + j\omega )

In Z-Transform, we work with polar coordinates:
( z = r e^{j\omega} )

r → distance from origin
\omega → angle with respect to real axis

Z-Transform definition:
( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

provided x[n] is summable.

metadata.section: DTFT and Z-Transform Relationship

pages.text:
Depending upon the value of r, the summation may converge or diverge.

Z-Transform is exactly equal to the Fourier Transform if we replace e^{j\omega} by z.

( X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j\omega n} )

Given a sequence x[n],

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} = Z\{x[n]\} )

Inverse relation:

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

If the Fourier Transform exists, then it must satisfy:

( FT\{x[n]\} = Z\{x[n]\} \big|_{z = e^{j\omega}} )

Sketch of representation in the z-plane:

( z = r e^{j\omega} )

The complex z-plane consists of a real axis (Re{z}) and an imaginary axis (Im{z}). A circle of radius r centered at the origin represents |z| = r.

The most important case is when r = 1.

In this case:

( z = e^{j\omega} )

which forms a circle of radius 1 in the z-plane.

( |z| = 1 )

This is called the unit circle.

pages.text:
Whatever we have studied in the Laplace Transform with reference to the j\omega-axis, we now replace that interpretation with reference to the unit circle. Inside the unit circle corresponds to one region and outside corresponds to another region.

The unit circle plays a significant role in the entire discussion of the Z-Transform.

For a given sequence x[n], if X(z) converges, then:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Substituting ( z = r e^{j\omega} ),

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] (r e^{j\omega})^{-n} )

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] r^{-n} e^{-j\omega n} )

Thus,

( X(z) = FT\{ x[n] r^{-n} \} )

Hence, the Fourier Transform of x[n] may not exist, but the Fourier Transform of the modified sequence x[n] r^{-n} may exist for an appropriate value of r.

Therefore, the focus shifts to the parameter r rather than only on \omega.

In the z-plane, the point ( z = r e^{j\omega} ) represents a circle of radius r. If r is constant, the locus forms a circle.

Evaluating on the unit circle:

( X(e^{j\omega}) = X(z) \big|_{z = e^{j\omega}} )

The existence of the Fourier Transform can be interpreted in terms of the Region of Convergence (ROC). If the ROC of X(z) includes the unit circle ( |z| = 1 ), then the Fourier Transform exists. Otherwise, the Fourier Transform does not exist.

pages.text:
For the Fourier Transform of x[n] to exist, the Region of Convergence (ROC) of X(z) must include the unit circle, that is, it must contain ( |z| = 1 ).

Example:

Let

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

where u[n] is the unit step sequence and n \geq 0.

The Z-Transform is:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n z^{-n} )

This can be written as:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (a z^{-1})^n )

This is a geometric series. A geometric series

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n )

converges if

( |r| < 1 ).

Here, r = a z^{-1}. Therefore, convergence requires:

( |a z^{-1}| < 1 )

which implies:

( |a| < |z| )

Thus, the Region of Convergence is:

( |z| > |a| )

In the z-plane, this corresponds to all points outside a circle of radius |a| centered at the origin.

Hence,

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Alternatively, multiplying numerator and denominator by z:

( X(z) = \frac{z}{z - a} )

This shows a pole at z = a.

The pole is located at z = a in the z-plane, and the ROC is the region outside the circle |z| = |a|.

Conclusion:

For the Fourier Transform to exist, the ROC must include the unit circle ( |z| = 1 ).

From the ROC condition ( |z| > |a| ), the unit circle will be included only if:

( |a| < 1 ).

Therefore, the Fourier Transform of x[n] = a^n u[n] exists only when ( |a| < 1 ).

pages.text:
Given the sequence:

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

we previously obtained:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > |a| ).

Special case:

Let ( a = 1 ).

Then:

( x[n] = u[n] )

The Z-Transform becomes:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z^{-1}} )

with ROC:

( |z| > 1 )

Thus, for x[n] = u[n], the Region of Convergence lies outside the unit circle.

Example:

Let

( x[n] = -a^n u[-n-1] )

This represents a left-sided sequence.

Compute the Z-Transform:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1} (-a^n) z^{-n} )

Rewrite the summation by changing the index. Let k = -n, where k runs from 1 to \infty.

Then:

( X(z) = - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a^{-k} z^{k} )

Rewrite as a geometric series:

( X(z) = - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (a^{-1} z)^k )

This is a geometric series of the form:

( \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} r^k ) = \frac{r}{1 - r}, provided ( |r| < 1 ).

Here, r = a^{-1} z.

Thus, convergence requires:

( |a^{-1} z| < 1 )

which implies:

( |z| < |a| )

Evaluating the summation:

( X(z) = - \frac{a^{-1} z}{1 - a^{-1} z} )

Simplifying:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

with ROC:

( |z| < |a| )

Thus, for this left-sided sequence, the Region of Convergence is inside a circle of radius |a|.

Conclusion:

For right-sided sequences such as a^n u[n], the ROC lies outside a circle.

For left-sided sequences such as -a^n u[-n-1], the ROC lies inside a circle.

For the left-sided case, the ROC is:

( |z| < |a| ).

pages.text:
From previous derivations:

For the right-sided sequence:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > |a| )

For the left-sided sequence:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| < |a| )

Thus, even though the algebraic expression of X(z) is the same, the Region of Convergence is different depending on the nature of the sequence.

Conclusion:

ROC of a difference equation is different for different sequences.

For right-sided sequences (RHS):

ROC is ( |z| > r )

For left-sided sequences (LHS):

ROC is ( |z| < r )

If a sequence is two-sided, then the ROC lies between two circles, provided the sequence converges in that region.

In general, the ROC does not include any poles.

Z-Transform is a linear operation.

If

( x[n] = a_1 x_1[n] + b_1 x_2[n] )

then

( X(z) = a_1 X_1(z) + b_1 X_2(z) )

and the ROC is at least the intersection of the individual ROCs of X_1(z) and X_2(z).

Example:

( x[n] = a^n u[n] + b^n u[n] )

where a and b are real numbers.

Using linearity:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} + \frac{1}{1 - b z^{-1}} )

The overall ROC is the intersection of the two ROCs:

( |z| > |a| ) and ( |z| > |b| )

Therefore, the combined ROC is:

( |z| > \max(|a|, |b|) ).

pages.text:
Consider the sequence:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} + \frac{1}{1 - b z^{-1}} )

The Region of Convergence (ROC) is:

( |z| > |a| ) and ( |z| > |b| )

Therefore, the combined ROC is:

( |z| > \max(|a|, |b|) )

In the z-plane, poles are located at z = a and z = b, and the ROC lies outside the outermost pole.

Properties of ROC:

1. ROC is a ring (annular region) in the z-plane.

2. ROC does not include any pole.

3. If x[n] is a finite-duration sequence, then its Z-Transform exists for all z except possibly z = 0 or z = \infty.

For finite-duration sequences, there is no question of convergence issues except at singular points.

ROC: All z except z = 0 and z = \infty.

Either one or both may be excluded depending on the sequence.

Example:

Suppose we have a right-sided sequence.

Case 1:

( X(z) = 1 + z^{-1} )

ROC: All z except possibly z = 0.

Case 2:

( X(z) = z + 1 + z^{-1} )

ROC: All z except possibly z = 0 and z = \infty.

Thus, for finite-duration sequences, the ROC is the entire z-plane except at isolated singularities.

pages.text:
Case (iii): Left-sided sequence

Consider:

( X(z) = z + 1 )

ROC: All z except possibly z = 0.

Next property:

If x[n] is a right-sided sequence and the Region of Convergence of X(z) includes the circle ( |z| = r_0 ), then the ROC includes all values of z such that ( |z| > r_0 ).

In particular, if x[n] is right-sided and the ROC includes the unit circle ( |z| = 1 ), then the ROC must be outside the unit circle.

Proof:

Given that X(z) converges for ( |z| = r_0 ), this implies:

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n] r_0^{-n}| < \infty )

Since x[n] is right-sided, n ranges from 0 to \infty.

Suppose convergence holds at ( |z| = r_0 ), that is:

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n]| r_0^{-n} < \infty )  ...(1)

Now consider any radius r such that r > r_0.

Then:

( r^{-n} < r_0^{-n} ) for all n \ge 0.

Thus:

( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n]| r^{-n} \le \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n]| r_0^{-n} )

Since the right-hand side is finite from (1), the series also converges for all r > r_0.

Therefore, if the Z-Transform converges for a particular radius r_0, it will also converge for all radii greater than r_0.

Hence, for right-sided sequences, the ROC is of the form:

( |z| > r_0 ).

metadata.title: Z-Transform
metadata.section: ROC Property for Right-Sided Sequences
all_explained_topics: Monotonic behavior with respect to r

pages.text:
Continuation of proof for right-sided sequences:

If n_0 = -m, then the summation can be split as:

( \sum_{n=-m}^{\infty} |x[n]| r^{-n} )

This can be written as the sum of two parts:

( \sum_{n=-m}^{-1} |x[n]| r^{-n} + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |x[n]| r^{-n} )

The second summation has already been shown to be finite under the convergence condition.

The first summation contains only a finite number of terms (since n ranges from -m to -1), and therefore it is finite.

Hence, the total summation is finite.

Thus, convergence extends outward for right-sided sequences.

Property (5):

If x[n] is a left-sided sequence and the ROC of X(z) includes ( |z| = r_0 ), then the ROC extends to all values of z such that:

( |z| < r_0 ).

Examples:

Right-sided example:

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

ROC: ( |z| > |a| )

Left-sided example:

( x[n] = -u[-n-1] )

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z^{-1}} )

ROC: ( |z| < 1 )

Case (6):

For two-sided sequences (bilateral sequences), if the Z-Transform converges, the ROC lies between two circles in the z-plane.

Thus, the ROC is of the form:

( r_1 < |z| < r_2 )

where r_1 and r_2 correspond to boundaries determined by poles.

Therefore, for bilateral sequences, the ROC is an annular region bounded by two circles.

pages.text:
Case (6): Finite-duration sequence

Consider a finite-duration sequence:

( x[n] = a^n , \quad 0 \le n \le N )

and

( x[n] = 0 , \quad \text{otherwise} )

The Region of Convergence (ROC) of a finite-duration sequence is all z except possibly z = 0 and z = \infty.

Compute the Z-Transform:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} a^n z^{-n} )

This can be written as:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} (a z^{-1})^n )

Using the finite geometric series formula:

( \sum_{n=0}^{N} r^n = \frac{1 - r^{N+1}}{1 - r} )

we obtain:

( X(z) = \frac{1 - (a z^{-1})^{N+1}}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Rewrite numerator and denominator in terms of z:

( X(z) = \frac{1 - a^{N+1} z^{-(N+1)}}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Multiply numerator and denominator by z^{N+1}:

( X(z) = \frac{z^{N+1} - a^{N+1}}{z^{N+1}(1 - a z^{-1})} )

Simplify denominator:

( 1 - a z^{-1} = \frac{z - a}{z} )

Thus:

( X(z) = \frac{z^{N+1} - a^{N+1}}{z^{N} (z - a)} )

This shows that:

• There is a pole at z = a.
• There are N zeros obtained from the roots of ( z^{N+1} - a^{N+1} = 0 ).

The equation

( z^{N+1} = a^{N+1} )

implies:

( z = a e^{j \frac{2\pi k}{N+1}} ), \quad k = 0, 1, 2, ..., N.

Thus, the zeros are equally spaced on a circle of radius |a| in the z-plane.

For finite-duration sequences, the ROC is the entire z-plane except possibly at z = 0 (if negative powers dominate) or z = \infty (if positive powers dominate).

pages.text:
Example: Two-sided sequence

Consider the sequence:

( x[n] = b^{|n|} ), where 0 < b < 1.

This is a two-sided sequence that decays exponentially on both sides of n = 0.

We can write the sequence as:

( x[n] = b^n u[n] + b^{-n} u[-n-1] )

For the right-sided part:

( Z\{ b^n u[n] \} = \frac{1}{1 - b z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > |b| )

For the left-sided part:

( Z\{ b^{-n} u[-n-1] \} = \frac{1}{1 - b^{-1} z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| < \frac{1}{|b|} )

Thus, the total Z-Transform is:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - b z^{-1}} + \frac{1}{1 - b^{-1} z^{-1}} )

The overall ROC is the intersection of the two individual ROCs:

( |b| < |z| < \frac{1}{|b|} )

Hence, the ROC is an annular region bounded by two circles of radii |b| and 1/|b|.

Since 0 < b < 1, we have:

( |b| < 1 < \frac{1}{|b|} )

Therefore, the unit circle ( |z| = 1 ) lies inside the ROC.

Conclusion:

Because the unit circle lies within the ROC, the Fourier Transform of x[n] = b^{|n|} exists.

If b > 1, then the unit circle would not lie inside the ROC, and the Fourier Transform would not exist.

pages.text:
Consider the expression:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - \frac{1}{2} z^{-1})(1 - 2 z^{-1})} )

This expression has poles at:

( z = \frac{1}{2} ) and ( z = 2 ).

From this algebraic form alone, the Region of Convergence (ROC) cannot be determined. The ROC depends on the nature of the corresponding time-domain sequence.

The poles are located at z = 1/2 and z = 2 in the z-plane.

Possible Regions of Convergence:

1. ( |z| > 2 )
   This corresponds to a right-sided sequence.

2. ( |z| < 1/2 )
   This corresponds to a left-sided sequence.

3. ( 1/2 < |z| < 2 )
   This corresponds to a two-sided (bilateral) sequence.

Thus, the same rational function X(z) can correspond to different time-domain sequences depending on the ROC.

Therefore, if X(z) is given only in terms of poles and zeros, the ROC must be specified explicitly to uniquely determine the corresponding sequence x[n].

Without specifying the ROC, the inverse Z-Transform is not uniquely defined.

pages.text:
Z-Transform Inversion

Given X(z), how do we determine x[n]?

If X(z) is evaluated on the unit circle, then:

( X(e^{j\omega}) )

This corresponds to the Fourier Transform of x[n], provided the Fourier Transform exists.

From Fourier inversion formula:

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} X(e^{j\omega}) e^{j\omega n} d\omega )

Now express the integral in terms of z.

Let:

( z = e^{j\omega} )

Then:

( dz = j e^{j\omega} d\omega )

Thus:

( d\omega = \frac{dz}{j z} )

Substitute into the inversion formula:

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int X(z) z^n \frac{dz}{j z} )

Simplifying:

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \int X(z) z^{n-1} dz )

The integration is taken over a closed contour in the z-plane corresponding to:

( |z| = 1 )

Thus, the inverse Z-Transform is given by the contour integral:

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \oint X(z) z^{n-1} dz )

where the contour lies within the Region of Convergence and encloses the origin.

Therefore, inversion of the Z-Transform can be performed using complex integration along a closed contour in the z-plane.

metadata.subject: Signal System
metadata.title: Z-Transform
metadata.section: Inverse Z-Transform Using Contour Integration

pages.text:
Inverse Z-Transform Using Residue Method

The inverse Z-Transform is given by the contour integral:

( x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \oint X(z) z^{n-1} dz )

where the contour lies inside the Region of Convergence.

If X(z) is a rational function, then inversion can be performed using the residue theorem.

Procedure:

If X(z) is expressed in partial fraction form, then:

( X(z) = \sum_{k} \frac{A_k}{z - z_k} )

Multiplying by z^{n-1}:

( X(z) z^{n-1} = \sum_{k} \frac{A_k z^{n-1}}{z - z_k} )

The contour integral picks up the residues at the poles enclosed by the contour.

Hence, x[n] is obtained by summing the residues of X(z) z^{n-1} at the poles lying inside the chosen contour.

Example:

Consider:

( X(z) = \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2} z^{-1}}{(1 + \frac{1}{2} z^{-1})(1 + \frac{1}{4} z^{-1})} )

Given ROC: ( |z| > \frac{1}{2} )

Rewrite the expression in a more convenient form:

( X(z) = \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2} z^{-1}}{(1 + \frac{1}{2} z^{-1})(1 + \frac{1}{4} z^{-1})} )

This can be decomposed using partial fractions:

( X(z) = \frac{4}{1 + \frac{1}{2} z^{-1}} - \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{4} z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > \frac{1}{2} ).

Using known Z-Transform pairs:

( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \leftrightarrow a^n u[n] )

we identify the corresponding time-domain sequences accordingly, considering the specified ROC.

metadata.subject: Signal System
metadata.title: Z-Transform
metadata.section: Residue Method and Partial Fraction Expansion

pages.text:
Continuation of Inverse Z-Transform Example

From partial fraction expansion, suppose we obtained:

( x[n] = -4 \left( -\frac{1}{2} \right)^n u[n] + 3 \left( -\frac{1}{4} \right)^n u[n] )

For the ROC:

( |z| > \frac{1}{2} )

If instead the ROC is:

( |z| < \frac{1}{2} )

then the corresponding time-domain sequence becomes left-sided, and we must interpret the terms accordingly using:

( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \leftrightarrow -a^n u[-n-1] )

Thus, the ROC determines whether the sequence is right-sided or left-sided.

Trick for Inverse Z-Transform:

If

( X(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} )

rewrite it in terms of z^{-1} as:

( X(z) = \frac{P(z^{-1})}{Q(z^{-1})} )

and expand using known geometric series formulas.

Case (1):

Consider:

( X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > |a| ).

We expand using geometric series:

( X(z) = 1 + a z^{-1} + a^2 z^{-2} + a^3 z^{-3} + \dots )

Thus:

( x[n] = a^n u[n] )

Case (2):

If ROC: ( |z| < |a| ),

rewrite as:

( X(z) = - \frac{z}{a} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \frac{z}{a}} )

Then expand in positive powers of z:

( X(z) = - \frac{z}{a} \left( 1 + \frac{z}{a} + \left( \frac{z}{a} \right)^2 + \dots \right) )

This yields:

( x[n] = - a^n u[-n-1] )

Hence, the same algebraic expression produces different sequences depending on the ROC.

Therefore, always check the ROC before performing inverse Z-Transform.

pages.text:
Properties of Z-Transform

1. Linearity

If

( x_1[n] \longleftrightarrow X_1(z) )

and

( x_2[n] \longleftrightarrow X_2(z) )

then for constants a and b:

( a x_1[n] + b x_2[n] \longleftrightarrow a X_1(z) + b X_2(z) )

The Region of Convergence (ROC) is at least the intersection of the individual ROCs of X_1(z) and X_2(z).

Example:

( a^n u[n] \longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| > |a| )

( a^n u[-n-1] \longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} ), with ROC: ( |z| < |a| )

If we take the difference:

( a^n u[n] - a^n u[-n-1] )

its Z-Transform becomes:

( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} - \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} )

Under appropriate ROC conditions, this can simplify to a rational expression representing an impulse sequence.

Time Shifting Property

If

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

then

( x[n - n_0] \longleftrightarrow z^{-n_0} X(z) )

The ROC remains the same except possibly at z = 0 or z = \infty.

Derivation:

Start with the definition:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Now consider:

( Z\{ x[n - n_0] \} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n - n_0] z^{-n} )

Let k = n - n_0, so that n = k + n_0.

Then:

( = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] z^{-(k + n_0)} )

( = z^{-n_0} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] z^{-k} )

( = z^{-n_0} X(z) )

Hence,

( x[n - n_0] \longleftrightarrow z^{-n_0} X(z) )

with ROC essentially unchanged except possibly at boundary points.

metadata.title: Z-Transform
metadata.section: Properties: Linearity and Time Shifting
all_explained_topics: Example of right and left sequences

pages.text:
Effect of Time Shifting on ROC

If n_0 > 0 and

( x[n - n_0] \longleftrightarrow z^{-n_0} X(z) )

then multiplying by z^{-n_0} introduces a pole at z = 0.

Thus, even though the ROC may originally include the origin, the introduction of a pole at z = 0 requires exclusion of the origin from the modified ROC.

If n_0 < 0, that is, for x[n + |n_0|],

( x[n - n_0] \longleftrightarrow z^{-n_0} X(z) )

with n_0 negative, we are effectively multiplying by a positive power of z.

In this case, we introduce zeros at the origin rather than poles.

Therefore, the ROC may include the origin unless cancellation occurs.

If a zero at z = 0 cancels a pole at z = 0, then cancellation may occur, and one must be careful while specifying the ROC.

Frequency Shifting Property

If

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

then

( e^{j\omega_0 n} x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z e^{-j\omega_0}) )

Derivation:

Start from the definition:

( Z\{ e^{j\omega_0 n} x[n] \} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{j\omega_0 n} z^{-n} )

Rewrite:

( = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] (z e^{-j\omega_0})^{-n} )

Thus:

( Z\{ e^{j\omega_0 n} x[n] \} = X(z e^{-j\omega_0}) )

If we evaluate on the unit circle, z = e^{j\omega}, then:

( X(z e^{-j\omega_0}) = X(e^{j(\omega - \omega_0)}) )

Hence, multiplication by e^{j\omega_0 n} in time corresponds to a frequency shift by \omega_0 in the frequency domain.

pages.text:
Effect of Frequency Shifting on ROC

The Region of Convergence (ROC) does not change under frequency shifting because the ROC depends on the magnitude |z| (distance from the origin) and not on the angle.

In general:

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

If we multiply by a complex exponential:

( e^{j\omega_0 n} x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z e^{-j\omega_0}) )

This represents a rotation in the z-plane. The poles and zeros rotate by an angle \omega_0, but their magnitudes remain unchanged.

Therefore, the ROC, which depends only on |z|, remains the same.

If X(z) has a pole at z = p, then after frequency shifting, the pole moves to:

( z = p e^{j\omega_0} )

Thus, poles and zeros are rotated in the complex plane.

Time Reversal Property

If

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

then

( x[-n] \longleftrightarrow X(z^{-1}) )

Derivation:

Start with the definition:

( Z\{ x[-n] \} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[-n] z^{-n} )

Let k = -n, so n = -k.

Then:

( = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] z^{k} )

( = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] (z^{-1})^{-k} )

( = X(z^{-1}) )

Effect on ROC:

If the original ROC is ( r_1 < |z| < r_2 ), then under time reversal, the ROC becomes:

( \frac{1}{r_2} < |z| < \frac{1}{r_1} ).

Thus, time reversal inverts the Region of Convergence with respect to the unit circle.

pages.text:
Convolution Property

If

( x[n] \longleftrightarrow X(z) )

and

( h[n] \longleftrightarrow H(z) )

then the convolution in time domain satisfies:

( Z\{ x[n] * h[n] \} = X(z) H(z) )

where

( (x * h)[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] h[n-k] )

The Region of Convergence is at least the intersection of the ROCs of X(z) and H(z).

Differentiation in the z-domain

Starting from the definition:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

Differentiate with respect to z:

( \frac{dX(z)}{dz} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] (-n) z^{-n-1} )

Multiply both sides by -z:

( -z \frac{dX(z)}{dz} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} n x[n] z^{-n} )

Thus,

( Z\{ n x[n] \} = -z \frac{dX(z)}{dz} )

This property allows computation of sequences multiplied by n using differentiation in the z-domain.

Application Example

Consider the known pair:

( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \longleftrightarrow a^n u[n] ), with ROC: ( |z| > |a| )

Using the differentiation property:

( Z\{ n a^n u[n] \} = -z \frac{d}{dz} \left( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \right) )

Compute the derivative:

( \frac{d}{dz} \left( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \right) = \frac{a z^{-2}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} )

Therefore:

( Z\{ n a^n u[n] \} = -z \cdot \frac{a z^{-2}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} )

Simplifying:

( Z\{ n a^n u[n] \} = \frac{a z^{-1}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} )

Hence,

( \frac{a z^{-1}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} \longleftrightarrow n a^n u[n] )

This demonstrates how differentiation in the z-domain corresponds to multiplication by n in the time domain.

pages.text:
Example (1):

Consider the sequence:

( x[n] = \frac{a^n u[n]}{n} )

Using known Z-transform pairs and properties, this can be related to logarithmic forms obtained from integration properties in the z-domain.

Example (2):

Given:

( \frac{a z^{-1}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} )

We know that:

( \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}} \longleftrightarrow a^n u[n] )

Using the differentiation property:

( Z\{ n a^n u[n] \} = \frac{a z^{-1}}{(1 - a z^{-1})^2} )

Thus, the above expression corresponds to:

( n a^n u[n] )

Initial Value Theorem (IVT)

Applicable for right-sided sequences where x[n] = 0 for n < 0.

The Z-transform is:

( X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n] z^{-n} )

As z \to \infty, all terms containing z^{-n} for n \ge 1 vanish.

Thus:

( \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) = x[0] )

Therefore, the Initial Value Theorem states:

( x[0] = \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) )

provided the limit exists.

If x[0] = 0, then the limit of X(z) as z \to \infty is zero.

Hence, the initial value of a right-sided sequence can be obtained directly from the behavior of X(z) at infinity.

pages.text:
Initial Value Theorem (continued)

From the Initial Value Theorem:

( x[0] = \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z) )

If X(z) is written as a rational function:

( X(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} )

and if x[0] is finite, then the degree of the denominator must be greater than or equal to the degree of the numerator so that the limit as z \to \infty remains finite.

Interpolation (analysis using impulse representation)

Any discrete-time sequence can be represented as a sum of scaled and shifted impulses:

( x[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] \delta[n - k] )

Taking Z-transform:

( Z\{ \delta[n - k] \} = z^{-k} )

Hence:

( X(z) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] z^{-k} )

For specific values:

If k = 0:

( \delta[n] \longleftrightarrow 1 )

If k = 1:

( \delta[n - 1] \longleftrightarrow z^{-1} )

Thus, each sample x[k] contributes a term x[k] z^{-k} in X(z).

Decimation (sampling every k-th value)

If we define a new sequence by retaining every k-th sample:

( w[n] = x[k n] )

Then its Z-transform is given by:

( W(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k n] z^{-n} )

This can be related to X(z) through substitution techniques and properties of powers of z.

In particular, when k = 2 (downsampling by 2), the transform relates to X(z^2) with appropriate scaling and consideration of aliasing effects.

Thus, decimation modifies the argument of the Z-transform and changes the spectral characteristics accordingly.
